name: Athenian Democracy
summary: Athenian democracy was the system by which the adult male citizens of Athens governed themselves in the fifth and fourth centuries BCE: they voted directly in the Assembly, filled the Council, juries and most magistracies by lot, paid citizens for public service, and held officials to account by audits and removal. Its own statements stress equality before the law, open debate, advancement by ability and every citizen's duty to take part. It excluded women, slaves and resident foreigners, restricted citizenship to those of citizen descent, and ruled an empire of subject allies.
scope: The constitution of classical Athens after Cleisthenes and Ephialtes, in its mature form from about 460 to 322 BCE (including the restoration of 403), as described by the Athenian Constitution and the speeches Thucydides reports, by Demosthenes and in funeral orations; Cartwright and the Stanford Encyclopedia define it as direct democracy for laws with sortition for officials. It is a form of government, so most statements on economics, society and technology are null. It excludes modern representative democracy (its own entry) and the critics of Athens such as Plato and Aristotle.

missingStatements.text: Public officials should have their conduct audited when they leave office.
missingStatements.rationale: Every Athenian magistrate rendered accounts to lot-chosen auditors and could be prosecuted before a jury afterwards, as Ath. Pol. 48, 54 and 55 set out.

quotes.text: to whom all persons who have held any office must give in their accounts
to audit the accounts of the magistrates for each prytany

missingStatements.declined: A procedural detail accepted almost everywhere today.

missingStatements.text: Citizens should be paid from public funds for the time public duties take them from their work.
missingStatements.rationale: Athens introduced and raised pay for Assembly attendance because the poor stayed away without it, and paid jurors and Councillors (Ath. Pol. 41, 62).

quotes.text: At first they refused to allow payment for attendance at the Assembly; but the result was that people did not attend.
the jurors at the law-courts receive three obols

missingStatements.declined: Accepted almost everywhere today, so not contested.

missingStatements.text: Citizens should be able to vote to exile a person who has become too powerful for a free state, without a trial.
missingStatements.rationale: Ostracism let the Assembly exile a man by popular vote against over-powerful individuals, a law Cleisthenes passed as a precaution against tyranny.

quotes.text: This had originally been passed as a precaution against men in high office
those individuals considered too powerful or dangerous to the city were exiled for 10 years by popular vote

missingStatements.declined: A historical institution that no one proposes today.

notes: Themes searched in the Athenian Constitution (parts 1-69), Thucydides (Pericles, Cleon, Diodotus, Athenagoras, Alcibiades), Demosthenes, Lysias II and the reference works: government, citizenship, law and courts, war and empire, alliances, religion, welfare and public pay, property and debt, gender and exclusion. The record is silent on economics beyond public finance, on technology, ecology and culture, which are null. The Athenian Constitution is a description by the Aristotelian school, used here as the record of institutions. Plato and Aristotle on democracy are critics and are not used.
